headline: AI-Proctored Exam Rocked by Cheating Scandal, Mexico's UNAM Orders Retake
deck: Mexico's largest university is forcing 58,000 applicants to retake an entrance exam after a surge in top scores pointed to widespread cheating on its AI-supervised remote test.
body: Widespread cheating allegations on a remotely administered, AI-proctored entrance exam have forced Mexico's largest university, UNAM, to order a mandatory in-person control test for nearly 58,000 applicants. The unprecedented decision stems from a drastic surge in top scores, raising serious questions about the integrity of digital proctoring technologies.

Nearly 160,000 prospective students took the highly competitive entrance exam using a lockdown browser and AI-powered webcam proctoring software. This system was intended to ensure fairness for applicants seeking admission to the National Autonomous University of Mexico.

Exam results revealed a striking anomaly: 16.3% of test takers scored 100 or more, a stark increase from the 3.5% observed between 2021 and 2025. The number of applicants achieving scores of 110 or higher jumped even more dramatically, from 0.9% in previous years to 5.5% this year.

Accusations of widespread cheating prompted UNAM to establish a commission of experts to investigate the suspicious results. The university sought to understand the root cause of the score inflation and uphold its rigorous academic standards.

The commission ultimately recommended administering a new control exam, which will be taken in person, to restore trust in the admissions process. This measure aims to ensure fairness and equity in access for all applicants.

Approximately 58,000 individuals will be affected by the upcoming control exam. This group includes those who initially secured a spot at UNAM based on this year’s test, alongside applicants who would have been admitted based on minimum successful scores since 2021.
The university rector apologized to honest applicants who will now have to prepare for and take the test again despite doing nothing wrong.

Evidence suggests that cheating was facilitated by a proliferation of tips circulating online before the exams went live this spring. These instructions included advice on how to access ChatGPT or other AI models during the remote examination.

The control exam will apply to all applicants who would have been admitted based on minimum successful scores in their program of study since 2021. While classes are currently scheduled to begin on August 10, details for the new in-person test are expected to be announced soon.

The incident at UNAM underscores the complex challenges of securing high-stakes remote examinations, particularly with the rapid evolution of AI tools. This situation demands a renewed focus on robust proctoring solutions and transparent processes to guarantee equitable access to higher education.
